newsitem.title: POLAND: DOCTORS SAY CARING PROTEST BITES ACROSS POLAND.
newsitem.headline: DOCTORS SAY CARING PROTEST BITES ACROSS POLAND.

text.p: Polish doctors launched an unusual protest for more pay and funding on Tuesday -- lavishing specialist care and costly drugs on their patients so as to strain tight public health sector resources.

Jacek Wutzow, deputy head of the protesting OZZL union which groups about a third of Poland's 90,000 doctors, said the action was getting 80-90 percent support in several provinces, while doctors in other areas were continuing with an earlier tactic of treating urgent cases only.
He told PAP news agency that if talks with the government on January 15 failed to bring progress, the protest could be stepped up further.
Wutzow said that the union urged doctors backing the new tactics to disregard spending guidelines set by officials.
"They should carry out full diagnostic procedures and inform patients of their rights as taxpayers," he said.
The tactic exasperated Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, who said that spending money unnecessarily would just harm the interests of patients and the health service.

"Luckily, this noisy protest involves merely a marginal part of the medical community," he told reporters, reflecting differences between officials and union chiefs over the extent of support for the protest.
The Solidarity union, Poland's largest, supports some of the protest's goals but has yet to decide whether to join in.
The doctors have called for budget spending on the health service to rise to six percent of gross domestic product this year, while the government has allocated 4.5 percent.
They seek a collective wage deal for doctors, which would increase their monthly salaries to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) -- three times the average industrial wage.
The health ministry argues that it does not have the resources to meet the doctors' pay demands but has boosted 1997 budget spending on health by a real 10 percent over 1996.

It also says a health insurance reform now passing through parliament, creating new special funds that will allocate money to hospitals according to their efficiency, will eventually benefit medical staff and the whole system.
